headline: Ziaur Rahman confined in 1975 coup attempt, leading to historic November 7th
summary: The confinement of Army Chief Ziaur Rahman on November 3, 1975, marked a pivotal moment in Bangladesh's tumultuous post-independence era, setting the stage for the events of November 7th.
details: On November 3, 1975, Army Chief Ziaur Rahman was confined at his residence by officers led by Chief of General Staff Khaled Mosharraf and Dhaka brigade commander Shafayat Jamil. His wife, Khaleda Zia, urgently informed Adjutant General Moinul Hossain Chowdhury about the situation.

Moinul Hossain Chowdhury found Ziaur Rahman under guard, confirming his detention. Zia was told he was a prisoner on the orders of Colonel Shafayat Jamil, part of a coup aimed at restoring discipline within the army.

This coup unfolded amidst the chaos following the assassination of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on August 15, 1975. The self-confessed killers had consolidated influence from Bangabhaban, with Khandaker Mushtaque Ahmad serving as president.
Many officers found the situation untenable, prompting Khaled Mosharraf's group to act. Their objective was to remove the August 15 rebels from Bangabhaban and curb their undue influence.

Khaled Mosharraf set conditions, including the unconditional surrender of the August 15 coup participants, Zia's removal as army chief, and a cabinet dissolution. Psychological pressure was applied with fighter jets and helicopters flying low over Bangabhaban.

Documentation from this period is scarce, with much of the understanding derived from personal recollections and testimonies. Accounts from individuals like Moinul Hossain Chowdhury and Shafayat Jamil shed light on these critical days.

headline_marked: [[Bangladesh LPG prices soar 52% since Feb]], 30-45% higher than neighbors
headline: Bangladesh LPG prices soar 52% since Feb, 30-45% higher than neighbors
summary: The official retail price of LPG has jumped from Tk 113 per kg in February to Tk 171.68 in November, driven by disrupted Middle Eastern supplies and increased freight costs from alternative sources like the US.
details: Consumers in Bangladesh are paying 30 to 45 percent more for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) than the official retail rates in Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Nepal. The official price in Bangladesh has surged by nearly 52% since February, rising from Tk 113 to Tk 171.68 per kg by November.

This sharp increase is largely due to the disruption of Middle Eastern supplies following the Iran war, which forced importers to seek LPG from more distant sources like the US. This shift has significantly pushed up freight costs and premiums for securing cargoes.

In contrast, over the same period, official retail prices rose by only 34% in Pakistan, 12% in Sri Lanka, and 7% in India. Nepal saw about a 6% increase, highlighting Bangladesh's disproportionate price hike compared to its neighbors.

Bangladesh faces structural disadvantages including relatively small purchasing volumes and heavy reliance on the spot market. Unlike India's large state-owned companies with long-term contracts, many Bangladeshi firms depend on volatile spot purchases, exposing them to price volatility.

The country also incurs additional costs for transferring LPG from large mother vessels to smaller ones before bringing it ashore. These factors, combined with longer shipping routes from the US (40-45 days versus two weeks from the Middle East), exacerbate costs.

Freight costs for US-origin cargoes have dramatically increased from around $82 per tonne before the conflict to as much as $250 per tonne under current conditions. The US share of Bangladesh's LPG imports rose from 27.4% in September 2022 to 85% in September 2023.
